main.text: [II, 510] [col. 1083] Chapter 7.
It is proved that שממית semamith in Prov. XXX, 28. is neither the ape nor the spider, but the stellio.

Of the four animals whose cleverness Solomon extols in XXX, 28., the last is שממית semamith, which he writes takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Over this animal there is a great dispute among the Hebrew doctors. Some explain it as תולעת של מטר, a rain-worm; others as שרץ של כנפים, a winged creeping thing, or שרץ מה מהעופים, some creeping thing of the number of those that fly. R. Jonah explains semamith by the Arabic word خطاف [khaṭṭāf] chottaph, that is, the swallow, as though it were the same as סנונית senunith, as the Chaldeans and the Talmudic doctors call the swallow. This is utterly absurd, since the swallow does not [col. 1084] have hands with which to handle and grasp, nor is it one of the small land creatures with which Solomon deals here: There are four, he says, little things of the earth. So this explanation has nothing sound in it. Aben Ezra, Emmanuel and Kabuenaki, to avoid these difficulties, preferred that שממית semamith be the ape, a most clever animal, a delight of kings, and furnished with hands like a man. But in my judgement it is too large to be counted בקטני ארץ among the little creatures, such as are the ant, the choerogryllius and the locust; for these are the examples Solomon used before. Some press in vain the resemblance of the word semamith to simia [ape]. For the name simia comes from nowhere else than from the simae [snub] noses. That is why the same animals were once called enares [noseless] ^{a)}, and the Πιθηκοῦσσαι [Pithēkoussai] of the Greeks are the Enariae islands of the Latins, as the distinguished Salmasius observes on Solinus. Quite otherwise think R. Levi, Kimchi and Elias: namely, that שממית semamith is the spider, which is accustomed to dwell in the towers of kings as much as in the huts of the poor, and there to weave its web with such skill of its feet that they can take the place of hands. So too the manuscript Arabic translator, who has here العنكبوت [al-ʿankabūt], the spider. To this interpretation Santes, Arias, Mercerus, Munster, Castalio, Junius, Tremellius, the English, Italian and Genevan versions, and any other more recent translators subscribe with complete agreement. But these men, by far the most skilled in the Hebrew language, ought to have observed that nowhere, neither in Scripture nor in the writings of the ancient Hebrews, is the spider called שממית semamith, but everywhere עכביש accabis, whence the Chaldee עכובית accobith and the Arabic عنكبوت [ʿankabūt] ancabuths, still in use today. Moreover, I admit that the feet of spiders are sometimes called fingers, as in the Frogs of Aristophanes, Act 5, [II, 511] Εἰλίσσετε δακτύλοις φάλαγγες ἰσότονα πηνίσματα [Eilissete daktylois phalanges isotona pēnismata],
Twist with your fingers, o spiders, the threads by which the weaver's beam is stretched. And in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 6, fable 2,
Thin fingers cling to her sides in place of legs.
And in Pisides' Hexaemeron, line 1152:

Τίς τοὺς ἀράχνας λεπτοδακτύλους πλάσας, Νήθειν διδάσκει, καὶ πρὸς ἔργα τοὺς μίτους Ἐκ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐντέρων ἀναπτύειν; [Tis tous arachnas leptodaktylous plasas, Nēthein didaskei, kai pros erga tous mitous Ek tōn par' autois enterōn anaptyein?]

Who teaches the spiders, made with slender fingers, to spin, and to spit out threads for their works from their own entrails? But one cannot find anyone who attributes hands to them. For although the spider's feet imitate fingers after a fashion, there is nothing in them that approaches the form of hands. Indeed, in Symphosius, Riddle 17, the spider expressly denies that it has any hands:
I have no hand, yet everything is done by my feet.

But granting, without conceding, that the spider's feet can be taken for hands because they perform the office of hands, the Divine Writer would still not have said that it takes hold with its hands, but that it spins, or weaves, or draws out threads: for that it handles and grasps with its feet is a slight matter, and shared with many animals; that it weaves is peculiar and θαυματῶδες [thaumatōdes]. Nor would he have said that it is in kings' palaces, since the filth of spiders does not well suit the elegance of a royal court. They rather dwell in the house of poor Euclio, in which
— — — there is nothing for thieves to gain, so filled is it with emptiness and spiders.

As Plautus writes in the Aulularia. Everyone knows the fable of the gout and the spider, who, they say, agreed that the former should dwell in the palaces of the rich and the latter in the hovels of the poor. Accordingly, when someone is said to have spiders in his house, or in his chest, or in his vessels, or in his purse, it is the same as saying that he lives in slender circumstances. Hence Afranius in Festus:
Is your little chest so full of spiders?
And Catullus, excusing himself to Fabullus for entertaining him, invited to dinner, less sumptuously:
— — — —, your Catullus's purse is full of cobwebs. [col. 1085]
Hence Hesiod, Works, line 473.

Ἐκ δ᾽ ἀγγέων ἐλάσειας ἀράχνια [Ek d᾽ angeōn elaseias arachnia], [II, 512] But you will drive the spiders out of the vessels, that is, emptiness and want. Accordingly the Scholiast explains it thus: Εἰ καλῶς ἀροτριάσεις, καὶ σπείρεις, ἁδροὺς ἕξεις στάχους (lege στάχυας). Ἐκ δὲ τῶν σιτοφόρων σου κιβωτίων τῶν μέχρι τότε κενῶν ἑστηκότων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀραχνιέντων, ἐξελάσειας τὰ ἀράχνια, καὶ ἐμπλήσεις δηλονότι ταῦτα τοῦ σίτου [Ei kalōs arotriaseis, kai speireis, hadrous hexeis stachous (lege stachyas). Ek de tōn sitophorōn sou kibōtiōn tōn mechri tote kenōn hestēkotōn, kai dia touto arachnientōn, exelaseias ta arachnia, kai emplēseis dēlonoti tauta tou sitou]; If you plough and sow well, you will have thick ears of grain; and from your grain vessels, which until then had been empty and therefore full of spiders, you will drive out the spiders, namely so that you may fill them with grain. Therefore it is hardly likely that Solomon assigned spiders a home in the palaces of kings.

What, then, will שממית semamith be? Plainly another animal, namely the stellio. This is proved by so many arguments that learned men weary themselves in vain seeking another interpretation, since this one is true and certain, and fits the passage best. As its authorities I have, first, the LXX translators, for whom שממית semamith is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], the stellio. For Mercerus, following the Complutensians, is mistaken in asserting that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] there is a kind of fish. Καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is indeed among the fishes, but also among the lizards. Both are in Hesychius: Καλαβώτης· ἰχθῦς ποῖος, καὶ σαῦρος [Kalabōtēs; ichthys poios, kai sauros]. Clearly καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is the same as ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs]. Hence at Levit. XI, 30. the Complutensian and Parisian editions have καλαβώτην [kalabōtēn] for the Hebrew הלטאה, where the others have ἀσκαλαβώτην [askalabōtēn]. Nor should anyone believe that the Greeks were so mad as to count a fish among ἐν ἐλαχίστοις ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [en elachistois epi tēs gēs]. 2. To the Greeks I add Jerome, in whom שממית semamith here is the stellio. 3. Also the Syriac translator, for whom ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, is the very same thing, as we proved abundantly above ^{b)} in the chapter on אנקה anaka. 4. As also the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha, with the order of the letters changed, as in forma [form] from μόρφη [morphē].

Moreover, that very word שממית semamith, for a kind of lizard, and indeed for the stellio, is known to us from elsewhere as well. For at Lev. XI, 30. one reads [?] or [?] semamitha in the Samaritan translator and in the two Chaldee ones, Jonathan and the other, named after the city: in the former for אנקה anaka, in the latter for לטאה letaa, where the Greek version has καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] and the Roman stellio. Finally, that the ancient Hebrews used it in this way is evident from what is read in the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 8, p. 77b: אימת שממית על העקרב, The terror of the semamith is upon the scorpion. By these words they indicate that this animal is a terror to the scorpion. Hence it appears that the semamith is not the spider. For no one has written that it carries on enmity with the scorpion or is a terror to it. But concerning the scorpion Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, says thus: The stellio is reported to be especially hostile to scorpions, so that even by its sight it brings them fear and a torpor of cold sweat. And Aelian, History [II, 513] book 6, chapter 22: Ἔχθιστα δὲ τῷ μὲν λέοντι πῦρ, καὶ ἀλεκτρυών· ὕαινα δὲ τῇ παρδάλει· σκορπίος δὲ ἀσκαλαβώτῃ, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει προαχθέντος οἱ τοῦ ζώου τοῦ προειρημένου [Echthista de tō men leonti pyr, kai alektryōn; hyaina de tē pardalei; skorpios de askalabōtē, narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei proachthentos hoi tou zōou tou proeirēmenou]; Most hostile to the lion are fire and the cock; the hyena to the panther; and the scorpion to the stellio, at whose approach it is seized with torpor. And Galen, On Theriac, to Piso, book 1, chapter 9: Ὁ οὖν ἀσκαλαβώτης, ὁραθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν σκορπίων, πήγνυσιν αὐτοὺς, καὶ οὕτως ἀναιρεῖ [Ho oun askalabōtēs, horatheis hypo tōn skorpiōn, pēgnysin autous, kai houtōs anairei]; The stellio, when seen by scorpions, stupefies them and so kills them. And Isidore, book 12, chapter 4: The stellio is reported to be so hostile to scorpions that, when it is seen, it brings them fear and terror. And Phile, chapter 29, from Aelian, wrongly read and understood:
— — — ἡ δ᾽ ὕαινα πάρδαλιν, Καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτην ὁ φθορεὺς κλὼψ σκορπίος, Νάρκη δὲ τοῦτον· — — — — — [hē d᾽ hyaina pardalin, Kai askalabōtēn ho phthoreus klōps skorpios, Narkē de touton]

And the hyena the panther (supply δυσμενῆ κρινεῖ [dysmenē krinei], considers hostile, which is to be repeated from the preceding [col. 1086]) and the thieving destroyer scorpion the stellio, but numbness seizes it. For in Aelian's words, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει [narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei], the word νάρκη [narkē] is not the torpedo [electric ray] fish, but the torpor [numbness] which seizes the scorpion when it sees the stellio. If, with some, you correct it to ναρκοῖ δὲ τοῦτον [narkoi de touton], but it (the scorpion) numbs it (the stellio), Phile would have said something utterly false, namely that the stellio is numbed by the scorpion, whereas on the contrary the stellio numbs the scorpion. Indeed Democritus, Pliny, Galen, Aëtius, Diophanes and others prescribe a stellio cut open, steeped in oil and left to putrefy, as an effective remedy against the stings of scorpions. Nor is it of slight weight that even today in the vulgar tongue of the Greeks the stellio is called σαμιαμίνθη [samiaminthē], a name plainly distorted from the Hebrew שממית semamith. The Glossae: Ἀσκαλαβώτης· τὸ σαμιαμίνθη [Askalabōtēs; to samiaminthē]. By Gesner it is written θαμιάμιθος [thamiamithos] and ψαμαμύθη [psamamythē]; by Bellonius SAMIAMITOS, who wrongly takes it for the Chalcidian lizard. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 1161.

There are some who write שׁממית schemamith with Shin, as if it came from שמם schamam, that is, to stupefy. This itself fits well the nature of the stellio, which stupefies the scorpion by its mere sight, as we have shown. But in Kimchi and in the purest copies of the Bible it is written שׂממית semamith with Sin Semol, just as סממית with Samech in the Talmudic writings and in the Samaritan paraphrase. Thus it is to be derived from סמם, not from שמם, that is, from poison, not from stupor. So, to understand the true reason for the name, one must know that two species of stellio are reported: one with a harmless bite, the other with a venomous one. The writers, however, do not agree in which places they are born. The Philosopher ^{c)} assigns the venomous ones to Italy and Sicily, the harmless ones to Greece. [II, 514] On the other hand Theophrastus, in Pliny, book 8, chapter 31, states that stellios, deadly in their bite in Greece, are harmless in Sicily. In Thrace too the stellio has a pernicious bite, as is found in Nicander. And Bustamantinus of Complutum asserts that stellios are so pernicious that, mixed by chance with food, they have laid waste entire populations. Hence Aëtius, Paulus and Avicenna prescribe so many remedies against the bite of the stellio. And Columella, book 10, chapter 7, wants the openings of beehives to be very narrow, lest the venomous stellio ravage the combs through the wider spaces of the entrance. He added the epithet venomous διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs], because another kind is harmless. The name stellio suits the venomous one better, if Verrius, in Varro and Festus, truly asserts that the stellio is so called because it drips venom. To the same was given the name סממית semamith, because סם sam among the Hebrews and Syrians is φάρμακον [pharmakon], or poison; and in Arabic سم [samm] samma is the verb to infect with poison. Therefore סממית semamith is properly σαῦρα φαρμακὶς [saura pharmakis], or φαρμακῖτις [pharmakitis]. I see that this very name is used by the Greeks in a sense little different. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 537:
Φαρμακίδος σαύρης πολυμήδεος, ἣν σαλαμάνδρην Κλείουσιν. — — — — — — — [Pharmakidos saurēs polymēdeos, hēn salamandrēn Kleiousin.]

You see that there the σαῦρα φαρμακίς [saura pharmakis] is the salamander, a kind of lizard so similar to the stellio that some take it for a species of stellio. Accordingly the Scholiast there: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα· εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra; eidos askalabōtou]. Yet in Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 4, ch. 52, the salamander, the stellio and the venomous lizard, in Greek σαῦρα φαρμακῖτις [saura pharmakitis], are different little animals, but very similar to one another. The salamander, he says, is an animal similar to the stellio, rougher, and more scaly than the venomous lizard. Perhaps by the name stellio he means only the harmless one, and by the name pharmacitis lizard, or venomous lizard, distinct from the salamander, the stellio with a harmful bite. Thus the pharmacitis lizard will be the same as the סממית semamith.

The same point is supported by the fact that the Arabs record two species of venomous stellio, which differ only in size. The larger is called سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, and the smaller [col. 1087] وزغة [wazagha] vvezga. In the name sammabras, compounded of سام [sām] and ابرص [abraṣ], the first part is shortened from semamith and means venomous; the second means leprous, or marked with spots of leprosy. So, literally, sammabras is leprous semamith, or a species of lizard notable for venom and for spots of leprosy. For two things are to be noted in the stellio: first, that it is venomous, which has already been treated; second, that it is leprous, that is, marked with spots as if of leprosy. The Arabic SAMMABRAS contains both of these, the Hebrew SEMAMITH only the first. Damir: وانما سمي هذا النوع سام ابرص لانه سم اي جعل الله فيه السم وجعله ابرص [wa-innamā summiya hādhā al-nawʿ sām abraṣ li-annahu summa ay jaʿala Allāh fīhi al-summ wa-jaʿalahu abraṣ] This species of lizard indeed has the name sammabras, [II, 515] because it is venomous, that is, God put venom in it, and (moreover) made it leprous ^{(1)}. The Romans called the stellio's spots by a more honourable name, stellae [stars], whence the animal itself is called stellio. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 5, fable 7:
— — — — and it has a name suited to its colour, its body starred with varied drops.

Salonius on Proverbs: What kind of animal is the stellio? A kind of lizard, very sluggish and of varied colour. ' Hence it got the name stellio, because it is marked and variegated as if with stellae, that is, drops. Here he follows the Poet in such a way that he seems to have taken stellae [stars] for stillae [drops], or guttae [drops]. By the opposite error many explain מרים Marjam, the Syrian name of Mary, as maris stella [star of the sea] instead of maris stilla [drop of the sea]. Pliny also calls them lentigines [freckles], when he writes of the Greek stellio in book 29, chapter 4: This one is full of freckles. Hence a freckled eunuch is called by Menander γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], that is, stellio, because of the spots on his face. Terence in the Eunuch ^{d)} wrongly rendered this colore mustelino [of weasel colour], as if γαλεώτης [galeōtēs] were named ἀπὸ τῆς γαλῆς [apo tēs galēs], that is, from the weasel, as Donatus observes there.

[II, 516] In Alkazuini, sammabras is defined as الوزغ الصغير الراس الطويل الذنب [al-wazagh al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs al-ṭawīl al-dhanab] alvvezgo (or stellio) with a small head and a long tail. In Damir and Alcamus, an animal من كبار الوزغ [min kibār al-wazagh] of the large guezgi, or stellios. The Arabs tell the fable that leprosy was inflicted on it as punishment for a crime it committed, namely because with its breath it kindled the fire into which Abraham was thrown. They add that leprosy is produced by eating salt in which it has rolled, or on which it has discharged slime. Hence this animal is most hateful to the Arabs ^{(2)}. And Iahius, son of Iamer, says that he holds dearer one who has killed a hundred stellios than one who has redeemed ماية رقبة [māya raqaba] a hundred necks, that is, a hundred slaves. Many sayings of Muhammad are cited on this matter. Nor was the stellio less hateful to the ancient Greeks. Antoninus Liberalis, in the passage cited above on the stellio: Ὑπὸ Θεῶν καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μεμίσηται· ὁ δ' ἀποκτείνας κεχαρισμένος γίνεται Δημῆτρι [Hypo Theōn kai hypo anthrōpōn memisētai; ho d' apokteinas kecharismenos ginetai Dēmētri]. It is hateful to gods and men; and he who kills it does a thing pleasing to Ceres. Yet it is useful for many things, which do not belong here. But I cannot fail to note what Alkazuini has in the chapter On sammabras: لحمه يوضع علي لسع العقرب ينفع نفعا بينا [laḥmuhu yūḍaʿ ʿalī lasʿ al-ʿaqrab yanfaʿ nafʿan bayyinan] Its flesh, when placed on a scorpion's [col. 1088] sting, is of evident benefit. So also Damir. It is thus established that it is the same animal as the stellio discussed above, although Avicenna sometimes uses the word for the common lizard.

Now, if what Solomon says of the semamith is examined, everything will be found to fit the stellio. There are four things, he says, little upon the earth (the Greeks ἐλάχιστα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [elachista epi tēs gēs]), yet wise, as if taught wisdom. Among these the stellio is rightly counted, a small animal and very clever ^{(3)}. On its small stature Ovid writes thus:
And it is contracted into a small form, lest it have great power to harm, and its size is less than a small lizard.
Claudian, or whoever is the author of the Sorrows of Ceres:
Spots appear, its form is small, a tail smeared on rises, and it imitates the wandering limbs of a tiny lizard.
Porphyry in Eusebius, book 5 of the Praeparatio, [II, 517] Ζώοισιν λεπτοίσι κατοικιδίοις σκαλαβώταις [Zōoisin leptoisi katoikidiois skalabōtais], To small little animals, domestic stellios.

There are many proofs of the stellio's skill. Hesychius, under Κωλώτης [Kōlōtēs], says that the stellio εὐστόχως ἅλλεσθαι περὶ τὰς μυίας [eustochōs hallesthai peri tas myias], leaps skilfully about flies; that is, in order to catch them. Phavorinus ineptly has περὶ τοὺς μῦς [peri tous mys], about mice: with which the stellio has nothing to do. But Augustine also speaks of flies in book 10 of the Confessions, chapter 35: What of it, when, as I sit at home, a stellio catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into its webs, often holds my attention? Theophrastus, in the book De anim. invid., adduces another proof, but a less certain one: Ὅτι ὁ γαλεώτης, φθονῶν τῆς ὠφελείας τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καταπίνει τὸ δέρμα, ὅταν ἐκδύηται· ἔστι γὰρ βοήθημα ἐπιλήπτῳ· [Hoti ho galeōtēs, phthonōn tēs ōpheleias tois anthrōpois, katapinei to derma, hotan ekdyētai; esti gar boēthēma epilēptō;] The stellio, begrudging men the benefit, devours its own skin as soon as it has shed it. For it helps those suffering from epilepsy. Antigonus has the same in the Mirabilia, chapter 24, and Apuleius in his first Apology for himself. And from this Pliny, book 30, chapter 10, concludes that no animal more deceitfully begrudges man. From the same source the names stelliones [swindlers] and stellionatus [fraud] were transferred into terms of abuse. There are also those who think that the Galeotae, the most skilful interpreters of portents in Sicily, took their name from the cleverness of this animal. To this Stephanus refers these words: Γαλεῶται μάντεων εἶδος Σικελῶν· Γαλεὸς δὲ, ὁ ἀσκαλαβώτης [Galeōtai manteōn eidos Sikelōn; Galeos de, ho askalabōtēs] (where for γαλεὸς [galeos] one should read γαλεώτης [galeōtēs]). But since in Hebrew גלה gala means to reveal, which is most characteristic of seers, I suspect that the name of the Galeotae is Hebrew, like a great many others which, as I have proved elsewhere, were carried over into Sicily with the colonies of the Phoenicians.

But Solomon himself amply proves the stellio's skill with these words: It takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Why he attributes hands to it is obscure to no one. Just as lacertus [lizard] is named from lacerti, that is, arms, so the stellio is called in Greek κωλώτης [kōlōtēs] from τοῖς κώλοις [tois kōlois]. Κῶλα [Kōla] are hands and feet. I call the forefeet hands together with Avicenna ^{e)}, who writes that غظاية [ghaẓāya] adhajam, that is, the salamander (in Avicenna's view), is preserved in honey only if it is gutted and يداها ورجلاها [yadāhā wa-rijlāhā] its hands and feet are cut off: where Dioscorides has φυλάσσεται ἐν μέλιτι ἐξεντεριθεῖσα, τῶν ποδῶν ἀφαιρεθέντων [phylassetai en meliti exenteritheisa, tōn podōn aphairethentōn]. If the salamander has hands, why not also the stellio, an animal very like the salamander? Thus Damir, in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] Chardaun, or On the land crocodile: له كف ككف الانسان مقسومة الاصابع الا انامل [lahu kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūmat al-aṣābiʿ illā anāmil] It has a hand like the hand of a man, with fingers divided into joints. Indeed, you may rightly call the feet of any lizard, especially [II, 518] the forefeet, hands, since they are like hands. Gesner, from his own observation: The lacertus is named from its likeness to the lacerti [arms] of a man, because their feet [col. 1089] are likewise split into fingers, as if from hollow hands or palms. The same: Very slender fingers, five in front and five behind, with little claws. On the hind feet the longest is the one that occupies the place of the index finger; the thumb is in a lower position, as in the hands of man: but the front feet have the thumb in the same position as the other fingers. You see that the forefeet, or more truly the arms, are in the shape of a human arm and hand, with the same number of fingers, and in the same position. How much better does the name hands suit such arms than the legs of spiders?

Now, the statement that the stellio takes hold with its hands I refer either to its walking or to its hunting. For when it walks upside down, hanging from a ceiling, it must either fix its little claws in small cracks or clasp with its hands whatever projects or is rough. That it walks upside down is asserted in express words by the Philosopher in the History, book 9, chapter 9, where he speaks of the woodpecker thus: Πορεύεται ὕπτιος καθάπερ οἱ ἀσκαλαβῶται [poreuetai hyptios kathaper hoi askalabōtai]; It walks upside down like stellios. And in the Marvels: Τὸν δρυοκολάπτην τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπὶ τῶν δένδρων βαδίζειν φασὶν ὥσπερ τοὺς ἀσκαλαβώτας, καὶ ὕπτιον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γαστέρα [ton dryokolaptēn to orneon epi tōn dendrōn badizein phasin hōsper tous askalabōtas, kai hyption, kai epi tēn gastera]; They say that the woodpecker walks on trees like stellios, upside down as well as face down. It is strange why Pliny renders ἀσκαλαβώτας [askalabōtas] as feles [cats], and ὕπτιον [hyption] as in subrectum [upright] instead of supinum [upside down], when he says in book 10, chapter 18, that the hollowers of trees (that is, δρυοκολάπτας [dryokolaptas], woodpeckers) climb upright in the manner of cats. All the more so since the same author, in book 29, chapter 4, acknowledges that the stellio is called in Greek colotes, ascalabotes and galeotes, so that no one should think Pliny was ignorant of the Greek names of the stellio. Similar is what we read in Plutarch's book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: that what the geographers teach is highly paradoxical, ἀντίποδας οἰκεῖν, ὥσπερ θρίπας, ἢ γαλεώτας, τραπέντα ἄνω τὰ κάτω, τῇ γῇ προϊσχομένους [antipodas oikein, hōsper thripas, ē galeōtas, trapenta anō ta katō, tē gē proischomenous], that antipodes inhabit the earth, who, like woodworms or stellios, with the lower parts of their bodies turned upward, cling to the earth. Here likewise the first translators had written feles [cats] instead of stelliones.

We have also said that the stellio uses its hands for hunting, when it catches flies or spiders. Bustamantinus: It seizes with hands that promise security. Indeed the deceitful feet, which were bound to serve for motion, take the place of hands and carry out the plunder; and to it the feet on which it rests in moving are hands, and the hands with which it seizes its prey are feet. Rightly therefore Solomon says, The stellio takes hold with its hands, whether it walks upside down or throws itself upon its prey. Both are marvellous and most worthy of note in a tiny creature. The Greeks have here Καλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδόμενος [Kalabōtēs chersin ereidomenos], and Jerome The stellio leans on its hands; the Arabic too has يتنسد بيديه [yatanassadu bi-yadayhi] it leans on its hands: as if referring this to walking. But no one could easily say what אקמתא דמסככה בידיה in the Chaldee means. For I do not [II, 519] understand what the Latin version means, The spider makes coverings with its hands. Nor much better is Gabriel, who rendered the same words of the Syriac paraphrase thus: The stellio, which creeps with its hands. I would rather read sepit [fences]; for סכך is to fence. But why the stellio should be said to fence, or to make coverings, I do not understand at all. Here too Drusius was at a loss in the Observations, book 10, chapter 6, and he suspects the passage of corruption. And instead of מסככה, fences or covers, he would sometimes read מסבכה, with Beth, entangling or making an intricate work, which would be said of the spider's web; sometimes מסמכה, leaning, which would be said of the stellio; so that the Chaldee would thus agree with the Greek and the Roman translators. But it is better to reconcile the Chaldee translator with the Hebrew text, in which תפש is to take hold. Accordingly Theodotion had rendered ἐλλαμβανόμενος [ellambanomenos]. I would therefore prefer to read, instead of מסככה mesacceca, מפככה mephacceca, Pe for Samech, letters not entirely dissimilar in shape. For פכך in Chaldee is the same as תפש in Hebrew, to take, to take hold. Thus Prov. V, 22. in the Venice edition: With the cords of his sins אתפכך, he is taken, or held fast.

Solomon adds that the semamith is in kings' palaces. This was the one objection that Mercerus had to raise [col. 1090]. "Our translator," he says, "renders semamith as stellio, which does not seem to fit, because it does not live in the courts of kings." But that the stellio lives in houses was not, I believe, unknown to this most learned man, since nearly all who have written about the stellio proclaim it with one voice. Thus in Eusebius, Porphyry speaks of κατοικιδίους σκαλαβώτας [katoikidious skalabōtas], domestic stellios. Suidas, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others among the Greeks define it as ζωΰφιον ἐοικὸς σαύρᾳ ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν οἰκημάτων ἀνέρπον [zōyphion eoikos saura en tois toichois tōn oikēmatōn anerpon], a little animal like a lizard, creeping along the walls of houses. So also Elluchasem, a physician of Baghdad, in his book On Animals: The stellio is a lizard that inhabits houses. Hence Kiranides calls it τοιχοβάτην [toichobatēn]. And in Spain the Catalans call it dragon de las casas, that is, dragon of the houses. That it lives especially in old buildings is reported by Niphus on Aristotle and by Ponzettus in his book On Poisons. But that it is also seen in new ones is asserted by Marcellinus in Hermolaus. According to the Philosopher ^{f)} it lives in mangers; according to Antoninus Liberalis ^{g)}, παρ᾽ ὀχετὸν [par᾽ ocheton], near drains; according to Pliny ^{h)}, about doors and windows, or in caves or tombs; according to Arnobius ^{i)}, it builds its nests under the hollows of statues. Matthiolus ^{k)} assigns to it the hollows of walls near the ground. But the ancients assign it ceiling panels and the vaults of roofs, where it may walk upside down. Accordingly, besides Aristophanes and Dioscorides, whom I have already cited above ^{l)}, you may also read in Avicenna ^{m)} that the stellio sometimes falls from above into a drink and turns it [II, 520] into poison if it dies in it ^{(4)}. These things, if I am not mistaken, amply prove that the stellio is not a wild animal but a domestic one. Further, I see no privilege by which royal houses should be immune from this pest. Indeed, the greater the pile and mass of stones in them, the deeper are the fissures and cracks in the walls. From this you may not unreasonably conclude that such little animals, which live mostly in holes in walls, dwell even more safely in the courts and palaces of kings than in a private house.

This lizard was carefully described by HASSELQUIST, Travels p. 356-358, under this name: Lacerta (Gecko) cauda tereti mediocri, pedibus cristatis, subtus longitudinaliter lamellosis [lizard (gecko) with a moderate, rounded tail, crested feet, lamellate lengthwise underneath]. "The body," he says, "the head and the feet are hairless and smooth. Very small, raised, shining points are scattered over the whole back. Very small pores run along the abdomen. Rather large, soft scales cover the very small space between the loins underneath. The back, head and tail are whitish above, with grey transverse spots scattered irregularly; the throat, abdomen and tail are whitish underneath." From these words it is clear enough that the name leprous was not undeservedly given to this lizard. Now hear the same Hasselquist on the animal's poison, from which it is called سام [sām]. "Most remarkable is this animal's poison, which it exhales from the lobes of its toes. The little animal seeks out places and any things soaked or tinged with sea salt; when it finds such a thing, it runs over it several times, and as it runs it leaves behind it a highly noxious poison. In Cairo, in July 1750, I saw two women and a girl close to death who had eaten fresh salted cheese, bought in the market, on which this little animal had deposited its poison. How acrid the exhalations of its toes are I once saw in Cairo, when the little animal ran over the hand of a certain monk who wanted to catch it: at once, over the whole area the animal had touched, very small pustules arose, with redness, heat and slight pain, exactly as in those who have touched a nettle." FORSKAL also mentions this lizard, in Descriptt. Animall. p. 13: "Lacerta Gecko. By the Egyptians it is called ابو برص [abū baraṣ], i.e. father of leprosy, or leprous; by the people of Aleppo Burs." Schultens, in Comment. ad Proverb. Chapter XXX. vs. 28. p. 486 b, interprets سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] as leprous breather, from سُمَام [sumām], which he says means pestilent blast.

Forskal p. 13: "The origin of the name among the Egyptians is amusing: if it lets its saliva drop into salt intended for use at table, it brings leprosy on the person who tastes it. For this reason they carefully cover the salt-cellar, or add garlic, which the lizard abhors. Others think the animal's name arose from the likeness of its colour to leprosy."
Book 2 of the Canon, ch. 2. عظاية [ʿaẓāya], which the Latin translator omitted.

Hasselquist on the gecko: "Locality: Cairo, where it is very common inside and outside houses." To him should be added Forskal, loc. cit.: "Common in houses at Cairo, roaming over the walls in summer. In winter it is not seen, but is said to hide in the roofs and to come out again in the middle of March."
